Your strawberry frosting containing FD&C Red No. 3 must stop being manufactured with that color additive by January 15, 2027. On that date, the removal of 21 CFR 74.303 (the listing authorizing FD&C Red No. 3 in food) takes effect, and all existing certificates for batches of FD&C Red No. 3 cease to be effective for use in food (90 FR 4628; 91 FR 50475). This means frosting manufactured and containing FD&C Red No. 3 that was incorporated while the certificate was still effective (i.e., before January 15, 2027) is NOT adulterated and may remain on shelves and be sold after that date. Only use of FD&C Red No. 3 after its certificate ceases to be effective (i.e., incorporating it into food on or after January 15, 2027) would render the food adulterated.

response.answer:
Under the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, codified at 21 CFR 101.65(d)), a food that does not qualify for one of the automatic exemptions (e.g., single-ingredient foods from encouraged food groups, or water/tea/coffee) must meet two main criteria to bear the 'healthy' claim:

1. **Food Group Equivalent (FGE) requirement**: The food must contain a specified amount of at least one food group equivalent from the food groups encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, lean meat/seafood/eggs/beans/peas/lentils/nuts/seeds). The specific FGE amounts vary by product category (individual food, mixed product, main dish, or meal) as set forth in 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v) and the associated tables. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(2)–(3); 89 FR 106064)

2. **Nutrient-to-Limit (NTL) requirement**: The food must not exceed specified limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, expressed as a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients. These limits also vary by product category. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v); 89 FR 106064; see also 90 FR 10592 at passage describing the rule as requiring 'FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients')

As summarized in the background section of 90 FR 10592 (Doc. 2025-03118): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients.'

response.answer: The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is governed by 21 CFR 101.65(d). This section defines the general nutritional claims paragraph that covers labeling claims using the term 'healthy' or related terms as implied nutrient content claims because they suggest that a food may help consumers maintain healthy dietary practices due to its nutrient content. The general framework for implied nutrient content claims is set out in 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), which defines an implied nutrient content claim as one that 'suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may be useful in maintaining healthy dietary practices, where there is also implied or explicit information about the nutrition content of the food (e.g., "healthy")' (passage cfr-21-101.13@2025-04-28#0000). The specific criteria for using the term 'healthy' are found in 21 CFR 101.65(d) (passages cfr-21-101.65@2024-12-01#0003 and cfr-21-101.65@2025-04-28#0003). The final rule updating the definition of 'healthy' was published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957), with an effective date of April 28, 2025 (as revised by Doc. 2025-03118), and a compliance date of February 25, 2028.

response.answer:
No, that was not a fair reading in mid-2025, and it is definitively incorrect now.

**What was true in mid-2025:** The January 2025 order revoking FD&C Red No. 3 (90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16, Doc. 2025-00830) was subject to an automatic administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) as of February 18, 2025, triggered by the filing of objections. During that stay, the effective dates of January 15, 2027 (food uses, removal of 21 CFR 74.303) and January 18, 2028 (ingested drugs, removal of 21 CFR 74.1303) were suspended pending FDA's resolution of the objections. However, the order itself was a final binding order — not a proposal — and the stay was a procedural pause, not a substantive reversal. The stay did not change the stated effective dates; it merely suspended their operation temporarily. Saying the removal was 'not final and might never take effect' overstated the situation: the order was final, and the stay would end either by FDA overruling the objections or by FDA modifying/revoking the order. The Delaney Clause finding (that FD&C Red No. 3 causes cancer in laboratory animals) left FDA essentially no discretion to reverse the revocation on the merits (90 FR 4628 at section VI, Doc. 2025-00830).

**What is the position now:** FDA published a final action on August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920) overruling all objections, denying requests for a public hearing, and lifting the administrative stay. The document explicitly confirms the original effective dates: January 15, 2027 for the repeal of § 74.303 (food) and January 18, 2028 for the repeal of § 74.1303 (ingested drugs). This constitutes 'final action on the objections' under section 701(e)(2) of the FD&C Act. The revocation is fully confirmed and binding.

Because no compliance date was separately stated in the January 2025 order, the operative deadlines are derived from the effective dates: food products containing FD&C Red No. 3 will be adulterated as of January 15, 2027, and ingested drugs containing it will be adulterated as of January 18, 2028 (Doc. 2025-00830, section VI; Doc. 2026-15920, section V).

response.answer:
The order published at 90 FR 4628 (Doc. 2025-00830, published 2025-01-16) changes three CFR provisions within 21 CFR Part 74, and they do NOT all change on the same day. The amendatory instructions are as follows:

1. **Amendatory Instruction 2 – Remove 21 CFR 74.303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for food use): This removes the entire listing that authorizes FD&C Red No. 3 as a color additive in food (including dietary supplements). Effective date: January 15, 2027 (confirmed per 91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920).

2. **Amendatory Instruction 3 – Revise 21 CFR 74.1303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for ingested drugs): Because § 74.1303 cross-references the identity and specifications in § 74.303(a)(1) and (b), the order revises § 74.1303 to incorporate that information directly, so it can stand alone after § 74.303 is removed. This revision takes effect on the same date as the removal of § 74.303: January 15, 2027 (90 FR 4628; 2025-00830#0021).

3. **Amendatory Instruction 4 – Remove 21 CFR 74.1303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for ingested drugs): This removes the listing that authorizes FD&C Red No. 3 in ingested drugs. Effective date: January 18, 2028 (confirmed per 91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920).

Thus, the provisions do NOT all change on the same day. The food-use revocation (removal of § 74.303) and the interim revision of § 74.1303 both take effect January 15, 2027, while the final removal of § 74.1303 takes effect January 18, 2028—approximately one year later.

The order sets no separate compliance date for any provision. Because the order is a revocation (not a new requirement with a phase-in), the operative deadline for each provision is derived from its effective date: once the listing is removed, any food or ingested drug containing FD&C Red No. 3 is adulterated (90 FR 4628, section VI; 2025-00830#0021).

The administrative stay that began February 18, 2025, was lifted August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920), and the original effective dates were confirmed without change.

response.answer: Under 21 CFR 101.65(a)(2), a 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim must be made in accordance with the general requirements for nutrient content claims in § 101.13, with one specific carve-out: § 101.13(h) is excepted when the nutrient content claim is made in accordance with paragraph (d) of § 101.65. Section 101.13(h) is the disclosure requirement that would otherwise mandate a statement such as 'See nutrition information for ___ content' when a food exceeds specified levels of fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, or sodium. This disclosure requirement does not apply to foods bearing the 'healthy' claim under § 101.65(d). All other provisions of § 101.13 — including requirements on claim type size (§ 101.13(f)), the general prohibition on nutrient content claims unless made in accordance with applicable regulations (§ 101.13(b)), and other general principles — remain applicable to a 'healthy' claim.

response.answer: Yes, your shelf-stable lentil soup labeled 'healthy' is affected by the updated definition of the term 'healthy' under the final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27). This rule revises 21 CFR 101.65(d) to establish new food-group-equivalent (FGE) and nutrient-to-limit (NTL) criteria for foods bearing the 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim. Under the new framework, your lentil soup would need to qualify under one of the pathways in § 101.65(d)(3): either as a food comprised solely of qualifying ingredients with no other added ingredients except water (paragraph (d)(3)(i)), or by meeting the applicable FGE and NTL requirements for individual foods (paragraph (d)(3)(ii)), or as a mixed product (paragraph (d)(3)(iii)), depending on its composition. Lentils are listed among the qualifying foods in paragraph (d)(3)(i)(E), but if your soup contains other added ingredients beyond those listed (e.g., salt, oil, seasonings), it would not qualify under the automatic pathway and would instead need to meet the FGE and NTL criteria (limits on added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium) for its applicable product category. The effective date of the rule is April 28, 2025 (as delayed by 90 FR 10592, Doc. 2025-03118). The compliance date is February 25, 2028, as stated in the final rule (89 FR 106064). This means you must conform your labeling to the new requirements by February 25, 2028; after that date, use of the 'healthy' claim on products that do not meet the updated criteria would be a misbranding violation. You may also voluntarily comply with the new definition before that date.

Once the effective date arrives, the listing in 21 CFR 74.303 is removed, and any food containing FD&C Red No. 3 becomes adulterated under the FD&C Act. The operative deadline is therefore derived from the effective date: January 15, 2027 for food uses (all provisions except amendatory instruction 4), and January 18, 2028 for ingested drug uses (removal of 21 CFR 74.1303). After January 15, 2027, food products colored with Red No. 3 may not legally be introduced into interstate commerce regardless of when they were manufactured or when inventory was acquired.

Importantly, an administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) was in effect from February 18, 2025 through August 5, 2026, but that stay has now ended and did not change the stated dates (timeline fact: 'dates_changed': false). The January 15, 2027 effective date for food uses remains operative.

In summary: there is no separately stated compliance date, but the effective date itself functions as the hard deadline. After that date, the color additive listing no longer exists and products containing it are adulterated. Your supplier's conclusion that there is 'no hard deadline' is incorrect.

The Red No. 3 revocation order (Document No. 2025-00830) was published in the Federal Register on January 16, 2025, at 90 FR 4628. This publication date is confirmed by both the order itself (90 FR 4628) and the subsequent order lifting the administrative stay (91 FR 50475, published August 5, 2026), which repeatedly references 'the order that published in the Federal Register of January 16, 2025 (90 FR 4628).' The date January 15, 2027 is the effective date for the food-use provisions, not the publication date.
